prompt: What is a key strength of relational databases?

options.text: Faster single-key lookups than any key-value store can offer
Flexible queries with joins, plus transactions and constraints
They scale writes horizontally out of the box with no sharding
No fixed schema, so each row can hold different fields freely

explanation: Joins, ACID multi-row transactions and constraints are the relational strengths. Key lookups are fast in both (not faster than a KV store), scaling writes takes deliberate sharding or distributed SQL, and relational tables have a declared schema.

prompt: What is the main cost of embedding customer data inside each order document?

options.text: Order documents grow so large that reading one order becomes slow
Customer data is duplicated, so updates touch many docs or go stale
Document stores can't nest objects more than one level deep
You can no longer fetch one order without also loading its customer

explanation: Embedding copies the customer into every order: fast single reads, but an address change must update many documents or accept old copies. Embedded customer data is small, documents nest freely, and fetching an order with its customer is the point of embedding, not a cost.

prompt: Which query can a pure key-value store NOT answer efficiently?

options.text: GET session:abc to load one session by its exact key
PUT cart:42 to overwrite one user's cart in a single write
Find every session of user 42, unless stored under its own key
DELETE flag:x to remove one feature flag after it's retired

explanation: Key-value stores only look up by key; a query by value (all sessions for a user) needs another key or index you maintain yourself. GET, PUT and DELETE by exact key are exactly what they do best.

prompt: In Cassandra, what does the clustering key control?

options.text: Which node in the ring stores the partition
The sort order of rows within a partition
Which columns are encrypted on disk at rest
How many replicas each partition is copied to

explanation: The partition key decides which node holds the data; the clustering key orders rows inside that partition. Encryption and replication factor are table or keyspace settings, not part of the key.

scenario: A chat app writes 200,000 messages a second. Every read is 'the latest 50 messages in conversation X'. There are no cross-conversation queries.

options.text: One large MySQL server with an index on (conversation_id, time)
A wide-column store partitioned by conversation, clustered by time
A graph database linking each message node to its conversation
A key-value store with one key that holds the full message list

explanation: Append-heavy, time-ordered reads per conversation at huge volume is the wide-column sweet spot. One MySQL server can't absorb 200,000 writes a second, a graph model adds nothing without relationship queries, and one key for everything is a giant hot key.

prompt: When does a graph database clearly beat relational joins?

options.text: Single-row lookups by ID across very large tables
Multi-hop relationship queries (three or more hops)
Summing one numeric column across millions of rows
Storing large binary files such as images or videos

explanation: Graph databases follow adjacency directly, avoiding the exploding join cost of many hops. ID lookups are fast in any indexed store, column sums are an analytics workload, and large files belong in object storage.

prompt: Which store should hold the ledger?
scenario: A fintech app moves money between accounts. A transfer must debit one account and credit another atomically, and balances must never go negative.

options.text: Redis, because in-memory writes keep transfers fastest
A relational database with transactions and constraints
A wide-column store tuned for eventual-consistency writes
A document store with each account in its own document

explanation: Money needs atomic multi-row updates and constraints like balance >= 0. Speed and write scale don't matter if a transfer can half-apply, and separate account documents without multi-document transactions can't debit and credit atomically.

scenario: A game updates 50,000 player scores a second and shows the top 100 on every screen.

options.text: Postgres running ORDER BY score LIMIT 100 on each request
Redis sorted sets (ZINCRBY, ZREVRANGE)
A graph database linking players who share a game match
Object storage holding one JSON file per player's score

explanation: Sorted sets keep scores ordered as they change, so increments and top-N reads are cheap. Sorting on every request at 50,000 updates a second overloads Postgres, a graph model doesn't help ranking, and object storage has no ordering or atomic increments.

prompt: Which are reasons to add a second database to a system? Select all that apply.

options.text: A pattern the main store serves poorly, like full-text search
A hot key-value workload such as user sessions
NoSQL is newer, so new features should start on it
Each service should own at least three databases

explanation: Add a store for an access pattern that needs it (polyglot persistence): full-text search or high-rate session lookups. Novelty and fixed rules of thumb aren't reasons, and every extra store adds operational cost.

prompt: What does 'schemaless' usually mean in practice?

options.text: There's no schema anywhere, so any shape of data is always fine
The schema lives in app code, which must handle every stored shape
The database infers a schema and validates every field on write
Documents can't change shape once the first one has been written

explanation: The structure still exists; it's enforced by application code instead of the database, which must cope with every document shape ever stored. Nothing validates for you by default, and documents can change shape freely.
